oi_lesson.objective: Understand how brain cell connections strengthen or weaken based on activity levels, known as neural plasticity.
oi_lesson.why_it_matters: Plasticity is the biological mechanism underlying learning and memory. For organoid intelligence, harnessing this flexibility allows living tissue computed in a lab to adapt, store information, and solve dynamic problems over time.
prerequisites: Brain cells communicate through specialized gaps called synapses.
Chemical signals trigger electrical changes in neighboring cells.
oi_lesson.simple_explanation: Think of brain connections like paths in a forest. If you walk the same path every single day, it becomes a clear, wide trail. If you stop walking on it, weeds grow over it and it fades away. In brain tissue, connections that fire together frequently become stronger and easier to activate next time, while unused connections weaken.
step_by_step: When a sending cell constantly activates a receiving cell, the receiving cell notices this teamwork.
Inside the receiving cell, chemical tags and building blocks are sent to that specific connection point.
The connection site grows physically larger and places more receptor tools on its surface.
Next time a signal arrives, the receiving cell responds much more strongly than before.
oi_lesson.technical_depth: At the cellular level, this is heavily driven by processes like Long-Term Potentiation (LTP) and Long-Term Depression (LTD). Repeated high-frequency stimulation causes calcium ions to flood into the receiving cell through special gates (such as NMDA receptors). This calcium surge activates enzymes that insert more chemical receptors into the cell wall, boosting future signal strength.
misconceptions: Misconception: Brain cells physically move around to form new partnerships when we learn. Fact: The cells mostly stay in place; instead, the microscopic contact points between them change in strength and size.

knowledge_check.question: What is the core idea behind neural plasticity?
knowledge_check.answer: Connections between brain cells change their strength based on how often they are used.

knowledge_check.question: What ion plays a major trigger role inside the cell during strengthening?
Why is plasticity important for organoid intelligence?
knowledge_check.answer: It is the physical basis that allows the living tissue to learn and adapt from experience.

oi_lesson.exercise: Draw two cells connected by a single line. Label one sending and one receiving. Now, draw a thick, bold line between them to represent repeated activity, and write down one short sentence describing what changed.
oi_lesson.summary: Neural plasticity allows brain connections to strengthen with frequent use and weaken with neglect, serving as the biological foundation for all learning and memory.

bci_lesson.objective: Learn how to clean raw EEG recordings by removing unwanted background noise and bodily artifacts using digital filters.
bci_lesson.why_it_matters: Brain signals measured at the scalp are extremely tiny and easily polluted by everyday body movements, which can trick a BCI into misinterpreting user intent.
prerequisites: Understanding how scalp electrodes capture electrical voltages (Day 6)
Basic knowledge of analog-to-digital conversion and sampling rates (Day 7)
bci_lesson.simple_explanation: When you record brain activity, you also accidentally record things you do not want, like blinking your eyes, clenching your jaw, or stray electricity from wall sockets. Filtering is like a digital sieve that lets the clean brain waves pass through while blocking out these unwanted signals, known as artifacts.
step_by_step: Identify the frequency range of your target brain wave, such as alpha waves which typically oscillate between 8 and 12 times per second.
Apply a high-pass filter to remove very slow, drifting baseline shifts caused by sweating or head movement.
Apply a low-pass filter to remove fast, high-frequency electrical noise originating from muscles.
Apply a notch filter to specifically target and eliminate the steady hum of standard electrical power grids (typically 50 or 60 Hertz).
bci_lesson.technical_depth: Digital filters alter the phase and amplitude of signals. Finite Impulse Response (FIR) filters offer linear phase preservation, ensuring that the time relationships between different brain wave components remain undistorted, whereas Infinite Impulse Response (IIR) filters are computationally efficient but can introduce phase distortion if not carefully designed.
misconceptions: Filtering can completely recover a brain signal that was totally buried under massive physical movement.
All electrical noise coming from the body is considered a true neurological signal.

knowledge_check.question: What is an artifact in EEG recording?
knowledge_check.answer: An unwanted electrical signal that does not originate from the brain, such as eye blinks or muscle tension.

knowledge_check.question: Which filter type is best for removing steady electrical outlet hum?
Why must we be careful when filtering EEG data?
knowledge_check.answer: Because overly aggressive filtering can accidentally distort or erase genuine, useful brain wave patterns.

bci_lesson.exercise: Examine a segment of raw EEG data containing a sharp spike caused by a deliberate eye blink, and note how it dwarfs the background brain rhythms in amplitude.
bci_lesson.summary: EEG signals are routinely contaminated by physical movements and environmental noise. Digital filters—such as high-pass, low-pass, and notch filters—allow BCI engineers to isolate clean neural data by selectively blocking these specific frequency bands of interference.

internship.topic: Explain sensor calibration and measurement error
internship.explanation: Sensors in robots and brain-computer interfaces never tell the exact truth. Measurement error is the difference between what the sensor reports and reality. It has two parts: bias, which is a constant offset (like a weighing scale starting at 1 kg instead of zero), and random noise, which bounces around unpredictably. Calibration is the process of adjusting your sensor readings using known reference points to cancel out bias.
internship.practical_example: Imagine an IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) sensor on a balancing robot. When sitting completely still on a flat table, it reports a tilt of 2 degrees instead of 0 degrees. That constant 2-degree shift is your bias error. During calibration, you record this offset and subtract 2 degrees from all future readings in your code.
internship.exercise: You are preparing a distance sensor for an automated delivery cart internship task. You place it exactly 50 cm away from a wall, but it reads 53 cm every single time you test it. What kind of error is this, and what simple math operation should you write in your embedded code to fix it?
internship.model_answer: This is a systematic error or bias because it is consistently off by the exact same amount (+3 cm). To fix it, you should subtract 3 cm from every raw measurement value your sensor gives you before using it in your navigation code.
internship.why_it_works: It directly targets the constant offset without overcomplicating things, making your distance measurements accurate right away for the robot's logic.
internship.improvement_tip: Do not just test at one distance. Test at multiple known points (e.g., 20 cm, 50 cm, 100 cm) to see if the error changes, which would mean you need a scaling factor instead of a simple subtraction.

linkedin.topic: Turn a project task into a measurable resume bullet without inventing numbers
linkedin.explanation: When writing bullet points for a robotics or embedded systems project, students often feel pressured to invent impressive numbers like 'improved speed by 50%' when they only ran a simple test. Instead of guessing metrics, you can use factual measurements you actually recorded during your university lab or personal project, such as compilation time, sensor polling frequency, or memory usage, without making up fake achievements.
linkedin.practical_example: Instead of writing a vague task like 'Worked on an Arduino line follower robot', focus on what you actually measured. If you timed how fast your sensor read data or tracked how much battery power your code used during a test, use those real observations.
linkedin.exercise: Look at one project on your resume involving an embedded system, robot, or BCI setup. Write down one task you did, then add a real, non-invented metric you actually observed during testing, such as loop execution time in milliseconds or sensor data update rate.
linkedin.model_answer: Programmed an ESP32 microcontroller in C++ to read infrared sensor data at 50 Hz for an autonomous navigation robot, keeping loop execution time under 20 milliseconds during lab tests.
linkedin.why_it_works: It uses concrete, truthful engineering details that you can actually prove if a recruiter asks about your code or lab test, avoiding fake numbers while still showing technical depth.
linkedin.improvement_tip: If you did not measure anything quantitative during your project, check your code logs, serial monitor outputs, or hardware datasheets to find real numbers before adding them to your LinkedIn profile.
